nicheStories.title: Can Cuba outlast Marco Rubio?
nicheStories.description: Shortly after four members of Congress returned from a fact-finding visit to Havana early last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a tranche of new sanctions against Cuba’s tourism, energy, trade and security sectors, the latest move in a months-long maximum pressure campaign intended to overthrow the island’s government by year’s end.Reps. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), Teresa Leger-Fernández (D-N.M.), Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.) and Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) heard first-hand from a diverse range of Cubans that the de facto fuel embargo and escalating secondary sanctions against foreign firms in Cuba are strangling the very people the U.S. claims to support. The group referred to the conditions they saw in the Cuban capital as a “silent Gaza,” contradicting the Trump administration’s claims that its brazen regime change gambit has only targeted the Cuban government.I accompanied the congressional delegation and have lived, worked and traveled to the island for over a decade. I can say confidently that, when the farmers, doctors, religious leaders, aid organizations, private entrepreneurs, and foreign diplomats with whom the members met say the crisis in Cuba is more dire than at any point in recent memory, they mean it. Nationwide blackouts are now a near-weekly phenomenon. With no electricity, access to running water is increasingly scarce. Children are not attending school because teachers can’t get to work. Neither can most workers, so private businesses are shuttering. With scant fuel and few international flights, tourism and the income it generates for independent Cubans are plummeting. Hospitals and clinics are running on fumes, as trash piles up on street corners, fueling mosquito-borne and viral illnesses. Food is spoiling in ports, fields and refrigerators, as Cubans see their rapidly devaluating local currency waste away to nothing.Add to that the near-constant threats of U.S. military action. Some are more overt, like increased U.S. surveillance flights off Cuban coasts and news reports of plans to send in the 101st Airborne Division; others are more implicit, like the recent indictment of Raúl Castro and the release of a State Department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the U.S. Cubans are living on edge, fearing that things will get worse before they improve.In this context, it’s hard to see how a diplomatic solution or a deal to resolve this slow-burning war of attrition — which Mexico, the Vatican, Panama, CARICOM, and the U.N. have all offered to mediate — could prevail.Still, direct talks between U.S. and Cuban authorities have occurred. The State Department’s Michael Kozak and Jeremy Lewin met with their Cuban counterparts on April 10. CIA Director John Ratcliffe met with Cuban intelligence officials on May 14. U.S. SOUTHCOM Commander Francis Donovan held fenceline meetings with top Cuban generals at Guantanamo Bay on May 29. Secretary Rubio himself has spoken and met with the grandson of former Cuban president Raúl Castro, Raul Guillermo Rodríguez Castro. Known as The Crab, Castro’s grandson has liaised with U.S. and foreign figures in Trump’s orbit, presented himself as a Cuban version of Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez, and even met recently with former Trump Organization executives in Havana, according to sources who have spoken with RS.Nonetheless, all signs indicate that progress in bilateral talks made back in March — when the U.S. “allowed” a Russian fuel tanker to dock in Havana, providing momentary relief for Cuba’s economy — has largely stalled, and other unconventional backchannels have petered out. A carefully hatched plan to send regular tankers of U.S. fuel to Cuba’s private sector was thwarted by Rubio within a day of its announcement, while Spanish hotel chains Meliá and Iberostar; French and German shipping companies CMA CGM and Hapag Lloyd; and U.S. credit card giants Visa and Mastercard have all suspended business on the island. It’s possible this could be all according to plan, and that a soft takeover of Cuba’s main industries by President Donald Trump and some of his friends and donors is in the works. After the largest foreign investor in Cuba, Canadian mining firm Sherritt International, announced its departure earlier this year, it said it would seek State Department approval to sell its stake in a nickel and cobalt joint venture to former Trump adviser Ray Washburne. An Australian gold mining firm recently followed a similar path, saying it’s also in talks with the State Department. With hundreds of prime hotels sitting near-empty, it’s plausible that U.S. hotel chains, including Trump’s, could snatch them up at basement-bargain prices. Fresh sanctions against Cuba’s military and state-run tourism companies have forced authorities to initiate privatizations of key assets, according to sources familiar with the matter. Emirati and Egyptian investors with apparent Trump connections are reportedly advising Cuban trade officials as they seek approval for the development of “Trump Island” on a largely military-administered cay in the northern-central part of the archipelago. And the container terminal at Cuba’s main Mariel Port and the leading international business center in Havana were both recently stripped of any military affiliation.Cuban, Cuban-American and foreign businesspeople are engaged in advanced talks to assume management or ownership of some of these properties, according to sources familiar with discussions. These transfers could provide an off-ramp that would effectively dismantle the Cuban military-led conglomerate GAESA and give private actors the upper hand in Cuba’s fuel markets. Yet Rubio, despite publicly seeking these objectives for years, is blocking even these workarounds.In recent statements, Rubio has said he would be realistic by accepting gradual economic change on the island and directly engaging with select Cuban leaders. Yet his actions indicate that his maximalist stance toward the island — demanding nothing short of drastic political transformation and wholesale privatization of entire industries — remains, even as Trump demonstrates a willingness to strike immediate deals he considers favorable to him and his allies. For now, Rubio seems intent on inducing economic dependence on the U.S. without precipitating outright collapse, cutting off every possible source of income to the Cuban economy while channeling the food, fuel, remittances and consumer goods that do enter the island through authorized Florida-based firms. The U.S. has also peppered in modest shipments of humanitarian assistance for thousands — not millions — of Cubans as part of a broader commitment to deliver $100m in aid through religious organizations over an unspecified period of time. The U.N. and Cuba’s allies in Vietnam, China, Mexico and Brazil have provided modest amounts of food, medical supplies and solar panels, but this aid is no substitute for the billions of dollars in trade and investment needed to reverse the precipitous decline in Cubans’ standard of living. Cuban authorities have sought to court that foreign capital by announcing the country’s most sweeping economic reforms in six decades, but these will have little immediate impact if not accompanied by the lifting of U.S. restrictions and the rollout of clear regulations providing potential investors with legal certainty. With Trump warning that “a lot of things are going to happen in Cuba in the next couple of months,” and with life in Cuba growing increasingly untenable, the Cuban people are running out of time. For now, their government is wagering that it can survive at least until next January, when Democrats will likely retake one or both chambers of Congress and seek to restrain further economic or military escalation against the island.“I don’t feel like there are any serious negotiations going on,” Rep. Pocan told a group of reporters in Washington on Tuesday. “We call on the Trump administration to… [engage] in serious and comprehensive negotiations with Cuban authorities that…provide a much-needed solution for a Cuban population that doesn’t have any more time to wait,” the four members jointly wrote.

nicheStories.title: Rubio arrives in Manila as China-Philippines tensions spike
nicheStories.description: The South China Sea’s waters turned choppy again just as U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Manila to attend an ASEAN summit. On Monday, a new maritime clash between China and the Philippines sparked mutual recriminations between Beijing and Manila and a mutual summoning of ambassadors. Washington too weighed in with tough remarks, denouncing Beijing’s “troubling pattern of provocation” in the South China Sea.If China indeed provoked this incident, its timing was poor. The gathering of so many diplomatic dignitaries in Manila at the annual ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ meeting gave the clash extra attention. Indeed, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi was also there, and his meeting with Rubio was apparently constructive. The maritime incident was discussed, with Rubio speaking of the need to manage the bilateral relationship between the two great powers. Since the Trump-Xi summit in May of this year, there is a deeper level of engagement between the United States and China, even as sharp differences remain.The maritime clash was significant for two other reasons. First, a Philippine naval crew member had to be hospitalized with a serious injury to his head after a Chinese sailor reportedly struck him with a baton. Serious injuries are rare in the recurring maritime incidents in the South China Sea; the last major one was in December 2025 near Sabina Shoal.Second, the brawl took place at Second Thomas Shoal, the site of a long-berthed Philippine naval ship that serves as an outpost for a handful of Manila’s marines stationed there. Second Thomas Shoal used to be the biggest flashpoint between Beijing and Manila. However, a bilateral agreement signed by Beijing and Manila almost two years ago greatly eased tensions over Philippine resupply missions to the aging ship and reduced Chinese coercive activity at the location. The agreement, limited as it is, was a victory for diplomacy. It is more than notable that it has held up for this long.Since the July 2024 agreement, other locations in the South China Sea, notably Scarborough Shoal, have been sites of clashes. The return of Second Thomas Shoal as a flashpoint would be bad news for the Philippines and Southeast Asia. The United States, which has a mutual defense pact with the Philippines, has an enduring interest in using its influence over both sides to shore up the rare diplomatic win and do its part in stabilizing the region. Rubio’s remaining day in Manila is an opportunity to both support an outgunned ally and find ways to lower temperatures in the South China Sea.

nicheStories.title: Pakistan thought it won the peace. Now, it could be dragged into war.
nicheStories.description: Four weeks ago, Pakistan looked like one of the biggest winners of the U.S.-Iran war.Its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, shuttled between Washington, Tehran and Gulf capitals for months. As part of his efforts, Pakistan hosted the first face-to-face U.S.-Iran talks in years and helped broker the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that Vice President JD Vance signed in June, thanking Munir and calling him one of the “very, very important people” in his life.Islamabad hired a Washington lobbying firm to convert that goodwill into defense cooperation and minerals investment, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif spoke of a “sun of progress and prosperity” for Pakistan’s chronically stressed economy after the MoU between the U.S.and Iran brought an end to major military operations.Pakistan's fortunes have since reversed. Fighting between Washington and Tehran has resumed, and Islamabad’s dual goals of being Iran’s trusted interlocutor and the Arab Gulf states’ security guarantor are once again at odds.President Donald Trump declared the deal was “over” in early July, after which the U.S. struck civilian and military targets in Iran. Iran, for its part, declared on July 18 through its deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, that it was “suspending all obligations” under the framework. The war has since widened into exactly the kind of multi-front regional conflict Pakistan spent the spring trying to prevent.The clearest new exposure for Pakistan is in Saudi Arabia, where Iran struck Prince Sultan Air Base at al-Kharj — its first direct hit on Saudi territory since March — just days after the Houthis, Iran’s Yemeni ally, fired missiles on the kingdom, hitting Abha airport in the country’s south. That escalation occurred after Saudi-allied forces hit Sanaa airport in Yemen to prevent the landing of an Iranian airliner; the U.S. Treasury alleged without providing evidence that the plane is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp. The strikes effectively enforced Riyadh’s airspace veto over the Houthi-controlled capital.Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact with Riyadh last year. It deployed fighter jets and thousands of troops to the kingdom after earlier Iranian strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure. More recently, Islamabad has reportedly communicated to Tehran directly that attacks on Saudi Arabia will be treated as attacks on Pakistan itself. Sharif’s own statement in the aftermath called the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia a violation of the kingdom’s sovereignty that Pakistan “strongly condemns,” pledging “unwavering support” for Riyadh's security.The tone is notable given that Pakistan’s parliament explicitly refused to get entangled in Yemen over a decade ago. In April 2015, faced with a nearly identical Saudi request to join the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, Pakistan’s National Assembly voted unanimously to “maintain neutrality.” Islamabad’s calculus has not changed. If anything, recent events have sharpened Pakistan’s desire to broker a lasting peace.Pakistan is home to the world’s second-largest Shia population after Iran, and the killing of Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, in February set off deadly unrest in Karachi and Islamabad; Munir himself had to intervene to calm a wave of processions and pledges of allegiance to the new supreme leader across Shia neighborhoods.Significantly, Munir and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif attended Khamenei’s funeral in July, and Sharif posted after that "the late Supreme Leader’s wisdom, leadership and profound influence on Iran and the wider region will be remembered for generations" — a demonstration of the fine line Pakistan’s leadership has to walk, one no doubt delivered with a domestic audience in mind as much as an Iranian one.That fine line becomes impossible to walk when a defense pact, triggered by Saudi-Houthi fighting or by further Iranian strikes on Saudi Arabia, would ask Pakistan to do the exact thing its parliament explicitly refused a decade ago: take a military side against a Houthi-Iran axis, and do so at a moment when its domestic Shia politics is highly combustible.Kuwait is now reportedly asking for the same kind of commitment that Saudi Arabia already has. Reuters reported last week that Islamabad is in early-stage talks with Kuwait — which has absorbed repeated Iranian strikes on its infrastructure in recent days — over an expanded defense agreement that would include "thousands of Pakistani troops on the ground, fighter jets, drones, an air defence system, and other defence-related facilities," according to an anonymous Pakistani government official cited in the report.Another anonymous Pakistani security official said the country “cannot consider a deployment of combat troops at this stage." That hesitation suggests that stacking multiple defense commitments across Gulf states in Iran’s crosshairs makes Islamabad’s balancing act much harder to sustain. Each new pact narrows the room to claim neutrality the next time Tehran calls.During this war, Pakistan discovered what happens when Gulf partners doubt its ability to balance between Tehran and the Arab Gulf states. The United Arab Emirates recalled a $3.5 billion loan in April and quietly began deporting Pakistani Shia workers by the thousands. The move was widely read as retaliation for Islamabad's perceived tilt toward Tehran during the mediation. Saudi Arabia stepped in with $3 billion to cover the gap, but the lesson was clear: Pakistan’s neutrality satisfies no one fully, and the cost of disappointing any single Gulf patron is measured in the billions of dollars.Economic self-preservation has been Pakistan’s primary motive for steering mediation and ending a war that has hobbled the economies of its creditors and choked the trade routes that power its own electric grid. Pakistan is on its 25th International Monetary Fund program; more than half of its tax revenue is put towards servicing its debts. It had barely stabilized its inflation before the Strait of Hormuz's closure sent rates back into double digits.In March, as the war’s first phase disrupted energy flows out of Hormuz, Islamabad ordered a two-week school closure and imposed a four-day work week to conserve fuel — measures the government has now indicated it may need to revive.A parallel disruption to the Red Sea, like the blockade of Saudi Arabia declared by the Houthis Monday, would be highly disruptive to Pakistan’s energy security, and by extension, its economy. While Pakistan imports the overwhelming majority of its fuel from the Gulf, the closing of another critical chokepoint would simultaneously tighten global tanker capacity and insurance costs everywhere, pushing the same spot-market prices Pakistan is already struggling to afford even higher.It would also add further pressure on Pakistan’s defense commitments to Saudi Arabia, given that Riyadh will not tolerate such a closure. In a recent statement, Riyadh pledged to deal with “Houthi threats against transiting vessels…firmly and swiftly.” The stakes for Saudi Arabia are high: Since the Strait of Hormuz was blocked, Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West pipeline to divert roughly 5 million barrels per day of crude to the Red Sea Port of Yanbu — its only viable export outlet while Hormuz is all but closed.None of this means Pakistan’s mediation was a mistake, or that its diplomatic capital has evaporated. Kuwait’s foreign minister still thanked Pakistan last week for its “constructive and mediatory role,” and Islamabad remains one of the few channels through which Washington and Tehran would resume talks, when the time comes. But the specific bet Pakistan made — that ending the war would allow it to bank the goodwill through commerce and financial aid — has not yet paid off.Instead, the restart of the war has brought Saudi Arabia back into Iran’s crosshairs. At the same time, the Saudi-Houthi front has reopened, the Strait of Hormuz has been closed again, and a blockade of Saudi-linked ships on the Red Sea has been formally declared.Each of these factors adds immense pressure on Pakistan, which now has every reason to double down on diplomacy, lest it be drawn in as a combatant.
